 [18 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
Handing Over 33 Hotels of ITDC to the Private Sector 
†*401.   SHRI   JANESHWAR   MISHRA:   Will   the   Minister  
of DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is scheme to hand over 33 hotels 
of ITDC to the private sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that many hotels out of them are 
earning profits; and 
(d) if so, the rationale behind this move? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING, STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE 
MINISTRY OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (d) A statement is 
Laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The Government has accepted the recommendations of 
Disinvestment Commission in regard to ITDC. So far as the 26 hotels 
of ITDC are concerned, the main recommendations of the 
Commission are as under: 
 Hotels situated in prime locations like Delhi and 
Banglore may be handed over to  established hotel chains 
through a competitive bidding process to be run on a long 
term structured contract on lease-cum-management basis. 
 Other hotels may be de-merged into separate corporate 
identities and the disinvestment in the companies will be 
through sale of 100% Government shareholding in them. 
The Government has also after examining the recommendations

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2000] 
of Disinvestment Commission, approved the disinvestment in the joint 
ventures with State Governments in respect of Ranchi Ashok Bihar 
Hotel Corporation and Utkal Ashok Hotel Corporation on stand alone 
basis. Consultations with State Governments are going on for 
disinvestment of ITDC equity in the remaining 5 joint ventures of 
ITDC. 
During the year 1999-2000 out of the 26 ITDC hotels, only two 
were in profit. Similarly, out of 7 joint venture hotels only 1 was in 
marginal profit during 1999-2000. However, the basis of 
recommendations of the Commission and the Government decision 
thereon is not based on profit or lo ss criteria, but taking into account 
various factors like, core & strategic nature of the sector, appropriate 
reorientation of public funds to match the priorities in accordance with 
the over all public needs, particularly for rural development and 
poverty alleviation rather than blocking limited resources of the state 
to such luxury sector where private sector has, over the period of past 
five decades, acquired better expertise and also is better placed to run 
the business given the very nature of it.

not able to withstand the competition; and

COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) The 
Government is aware of the concerns of Indian industry regarding 
import of cheap goods from China and has taken following steps in 
this regard: 
• The Directorate General of Anti-Dumping & Allied Duties has 
initiated suo-moto investigations against the imports of Dry 
Battery, Toys and Sports Shoes, which are items mainly 
produced by the small-scale sector.

domestic goods. For complian ce of this requirement all 
manufacturers/exporters of these products to India shall be 
required to . register themselves with Bureau of Indian 
Standards (BIS). The list of 131 products include various food

and Measures (Packaged Commodity) Order 1977, as applicable 
on domestic producers.

outdated machinery & obsolete tech nology, poor infrastructure, lack 
of access to markets, competition from allied products, and 
competition from competing imports. Government has initiated 
following measures to enable sma ll scale industries overcome these 
problems and withstand competition; 
• Announcement of a new Credit Insurance Scheme in the  
Budget (1999-2000) for providing adequate security to banks

financial intermediaries for pur poses of on lending to the tiny

67 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2000] 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor;

World Trade Organisation (WTO); and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to 
(f) USA banned import of shrimps harvested through a manner which 
adversely affects certain sea turtles under the provisions of Section 
609 of US Public Law 101—162 with effect from 1.5.1996. The 
principal requirement under the US law was the use of Turtle Excluder 
Devices (TEDs) in shrimp trawls which prevents incidental catch of 
sea turtles. The US Government further provided that consequent to 
the ban, all shrimp and shrimp products entering US should be 
accompanied by a declaration (DSP 121) to the effect that shrimp 
consignment accompanying the declaration was harvested under the 
conditions that do not adversely affect sea turtles. 
Government have authorised the Marine Products Exports 
Development Authority (MPEDA) to issue such declaration clarifying 
that shrimp being exported had been sourced from aquaculture or 
harvested by using non- mechanical or traditio nal means and exports 
are effected accordingly. 
India along with Malaysia, Thailand and Pakistan approached 
Dispute Settlement Body of the World Trade Organisation, seeking 
establishment of a Panel. The Panel decided the case in favour of India 
and other appealing countries, against which the US filed an appeal. 
The Appellate Body decided that the Dispute Settlement Body should 
request the US to bring its measures in conformity with US obligations 
under the GATT. The USA have revised their guidelines on 
implementing Section 609 of Public Law. However, the restrictions 
imposed on imports remain in force. Our exports continue to be 
allowed accompanied by the DSP-121 Declaration.

3026. DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA: Will the Minister of

item captioned "Fakes a genuine problem" which appeared in the

MRP as genuine brands and look-a like products not only hurt the 
credibility of the company that owns the brand name but the 
counterfeit is hard to detect and Government too lose tax revenue;

the sale of such products in the market in order to save the consumer 
and loss of revenue to exchequer too? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Infringement of a registered trademark, through unauthorized 
use, affects the goodwill enjoyed by the genuine trademark owner in 
that the quality assurance inherent in the original trademark is not 
made available to the consumer. The Trade & Merchandise Marks 
Act, 1958 provides safeguards to registered trademark owners against 
such abusive use of trademarks. Cases of application of genuine trade 
marks on sub-standard items or those not conforming to specifications 
would, however, be covered under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, 
being administered by the Department of Consumer Affairs. 
(c) The Trade & Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 provides penalties 
for infringement, falsification etc. of trademarks. These are being 
further enhanced under the to-be-operationalized Trade Marks Act, 
1999 in order to provide adequate deterrent against the misuse of the 
88

trademark. Under the Trade & Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, the 
onus of initiating action against infr ingement of trademarks lies upon 
the owner of the registered trademark who can move the civil or 
criminal court for redressal. Affected consumers can also seek 
redressal/relief against sale of counterfeit goods under the Consumer 
Protection Act, 1986.

3066. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: SHRI 
SURESH KALMADI: 
Will the Minister of INFO RMATION AND BROADCASTING be

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) Ail advertisements of 
Doordarshan are governed by Code for Commercial Advertisements 
which inter-alia prohibits any advertisements depicting consumption 
of cigarettes, liquor and tobacco. 
All programmes and advertisemen ts of satellite TV channels, 
when re-transmitted through cable ne twork, are required to adhere to 
the Programme and advertisement Codes prescribed under Cable 
Television Networks (Regulatio ns) Act, 1995 and Rules framed 
thereunder as amended from time to time. The Rules prohibit 
advertisement of liquor and tobacco  products on satellite channels 
when transmitted through cable networks. 
Films/Advertisement, for public e xhibition in India, are certified 
by the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) as per the 
guidelines laid by them. The guidelines seek to ensure that scenes 
justifying or glorifying drinking or smoking and consumption of 
tobacco arc not shown. 
The Directorate of Advertising and Visual Publicity has been 
issuing press advertisements and producing audio/video spots on the 
ill-effects of cigarette, tobacco and liquor on behalf of the Ministry of 
Health/Central Health Education Bureau. 
In matters relating to the Pres s, the Government pursues the 
policy of non-interferencc so as to uphold the freedom of the Press. 
Government docs not monitor the Print Media. The Press Council of 
India, an autonomous statutory body set up to preserve the freedom of 
the press and improve the standards of Newspapers and News 
agencies in India, has also not laid down any code of ethics for the 
journalists for reporting/advertisements of cigarettes, tobacco and

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA 
GANDHI): (a) No, Sir. The practice of untouchability is rather non 
existent in some States/UTs. namely, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, 
Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, West 
Bengal, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh Admn., Daman & 
Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, and La kshadweep. However it exists in

Maharashtra, Orissa, Pu njab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh,

Tribes has informed that it brings  out details in its various Reports 
indicating the number of cases registered under the Protection of Civil 
Rights Act, 1955 which retatc to th e practice of untouchability. As per 
the provisions of the Act, untouchability cases arc registered 
164

Courts have been set up for trying the cases under the Protection of 
Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Sche duled Castes and the Scheduled

(c) and (d) Following steps have been taken for enforcement of 
the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 in an effective manner. 
(i) Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme, Central assistance is 
provided to the State Goverments on 50:50 basis and to Union 
Territory Administrations on 100% basis for measures 
undertaken by them which include the provision of adequate

initiating or exercising supervis ion over prosecution, setting

surveys and identification of untouchability prone areas.

2-2000 for ensuring effective implementation of provisions of 
the act and policies as also the delivery of services and 
justice to the victims and target group.

3109. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of

(c) An urban agglomeration is a continuous urban spread 
comprising a town and its adjoining urban outgrowths (OGS), or two 
or more physically contiguous towns and any adjoining urban 
outgrowths of such towns. In some  cases, railway colonies, university 
campuses, port areas, military camps,  etc. would have come up near 
a city or town outside its statutory limits but within the revenue limits 
of a village for villages contiguous to the town. Each such individual 
area by itself may not satisfy the minimum population limit to qualify 
it to be treated as an independent  urban unit but may deserve to be 
clubbed with the towns as a continuous urban spread. 
The following are the possible different situations in which urban 
agglomerations would be constituted:—  
(i) a city or town with one or more contiguous outgrowths: 
(ii) two or more adjoining towns with their outgrowths; and 
(iii) a city and one or more adjoining towns with their outgrowths 
all of which form a continuous spread. 
The Registrar General of India has reported that the above 
definition was uniformly applied for delineation of urban 
agglomerations in the country.

STRATEGY FOR URBAN INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT 
The Central Government is taking following actions to facilitate 
flow of funds in the urban infrastructure sector. 
1. CENTRAL   SCHEMES   FOR   URBAN   INFRASTRUCTURE 
DEVELOPMENT: 
For strengthening of urban infrastructure in small and medium 
towns as well as in metros, the Central Government has the twin 
schemes of INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF SMALL & 
MEDIUM TOWNS (IDSMT) and MEGA CITY SCHEMES. 
2. DEVELOPMENT OF SATELLITE TOWNSHIPS:  
With a view to progressive decentralization of various 
administrative and economic activities concentrated in Delhi and their 
dispersal to satellite towns, a NATIONAL CAPITAL REGIONAL 
PLAN has been formulated by the Central Government, so as to 
contain the Delhi's population within manageable limits. 
3. FISCAL CONCESSIONS FOR ATTRACTING INVESTMENT 
IN URBAN INFRASTRUCTURE: 
In order to attract substantial in vestments for urban infrastructure 
development  particularly from  the  private, sector a 
number of fiscal concessions have been announced. 
4. FOREIGN DIRECT INVESTMENT (FDI):  
Till now Foreign Direct Investment in urban services was allowed 
by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) on a case to case 
basis. In line with the Government's Policy declareation of Policy 
2000 for increased Foreign Direct In vestment (FDI) in manufacturing 
sector, there is now no bar on FDI in urban infrastructure facilities, 
which are open to FDI both under FIBP and the automatic route as per 
sector specific guidelines. 
5. EXTERNAL ASSISTANCE:  
In India external aid in urban sector is a recent phenomena and it 
has not only been very limited but also restricted to only few 
211 

RAJYA SABHA        [18 December, 2000] 
components of urban infrastructure, primarily going to 3 to 4 States 
only. Central Government has with a view to cover all sectors in an 
integrated fashion and to cover all States have recently negotiated a 
line of credit of US 200 million from the Asian Development Bank as 
part of Urban and Environmental Infr astructure Facility Project. This 
loan will be chennalised through HUDCO, ICICI and IDFC over a 
period of 3 years. This financial facility will be available for 
commercially viable urban infrastructure projects. 
Foreign aid agencies like The World Bank and the Asian 
Development Bank have already funded a number of projects. 
6. TRAINING: 
A National level Training Polic y outlining the methodology of 
training of different municipal levels so as to strengthen the Urban 
Local Bodies by developing technical expertise would be a necessity. 
It would require development of Training capsules for involving all 
institutions across the country. The training would be required for not 
just the different levels of muni cipal administration but also non-
officials and other stakeholders involved in the process of urban 
services provisioning. In this entire process, the Institutions across the 
country would network with each creating an Apex Training 
Institution supported by Regional and State level Institutions. The key 
areas of training would include: 
—-Municipal Finance and Accounting  
—Management of Urban Services  
—Urban Infrastructure Financing  
—Municipal Resource mobilisation  
—Privatisation, Pricing and Cost Recovery  
—Urban Environment Management  
—City development strategics  
—Municipal Information System  
Administration of municipalities being a complex subject, the 
creation of a separate cadre of "urban managers" needs to be evolved 
over .time, through appropriate training and a dedicated 
Institution/Academy would have to be created. This capacity building 
exercise  would  held  improve  the  existing  scenario  and  thereby 
212

promote investments in the sector since the local bodies would now be 
empowered and in a state of preparedness to take on the role 
envisaged for them.

News-Item "Ground, Supply water highly contaminated" 
3142. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether attention of Government has been drawn to the news-
item captioned "Ground, supply water highly contaminated" as reported 
in the Hindustan Times, dated 20th September, 2000; 
(b) if so, whether the drinking wate r available for the citizens of 
Delhi is highly contaminated with Nitrates, Fluoride, Ammonia and 
coliform; 
(c) if so, whether Government in consultation with the State 
Government propose to chalk out scheme to make available drinking 
water free from any contamination; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND 
POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) Government 
are aware of the report. 
(b) The Delhi Jal Board had report ed that out of total potable 
water supplied, only 12% is ground water. About 6 MGD ground water 
obtained through Renney wells in being treated at Okhla water Works, 
rest of the ground water obtained from tubewells is supplied after 
chlorination. The quality of ground  water supplied is being checked 
regularly and potable water is supplied. Whenever a ground water 
source is found unfit for drinking, the same is closed and drinking 
water is supplied through alternative sources. 
According to the Delhi Jal Board, the drinking water being 
supplied by them is safe, potable and conforms to the standards laid 
down by the Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty Alleviation 
and Bureau of Indian Standards (IS 10500/91). The quality of water is 
being closely monitored samples are lifted and checked right from 
water treatment plants to consumer's  point. Field  Engineers  also 
check water quality  at the  consumer end.

Whenever   any   deficiency   is   noticed,   prompt   remedial   action   is 
taken and till then potable water is supplied through tankers. 
(c) and (d) The Govt, of NCT of Delhi is in the process of seeking 
World Bank assistance for reorganisation of water supply and 
sanitation facilities in Delhi at an es timated cost of Rs. 1624.50 crores. 
Delhi Govt, has already signed an agreement with World Bank for 
availing US $ 25 million under Project Preparation Facility. In the 
meanwhile the Delhi Jal Board is also taking action for replacing 
old/damaged/corroded pipes in a phased manner. During the year 
1999-2000, 114 kms. lines has been replaced. There is a target to 
replace 200 Kms. of such water lines during this year, out of which 97 
Kms. has been replaced.

MOTION EXPRESSING DISAGREEMENT WITH REPORTED 
STATEMENT OF THE PRIME MINISTER IN REGARD TO 
THREE MINISTERS OF THE UNION CABINETAGAINST 
WHOM CBI HAS COMPLETED INVESTIGATIONS AND FILED 
CHARGE SHEETS 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal) Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, with your permission, I beg to move the following 
motion: 
"That this House expresses its disagreement with the 
reported statement of the Prime Minister in which he has 
given a clean chit to three Ministers of the Union Cabinet, 
namely, Shri LK. Advani, Dr. Murli Manohar Joshi and 
Sushree Uma Bharati, against whom the CBI has 
completed investigations and filed charge sheets, and 
through this statement the Prime Minister has prejudged 
the issue". 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR (Maharashtra): Sir, I wish to 
raise a point of order. 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR (Gujarat) : You quote the rule. ... 
(Interruptions)... 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: Please don't shout. I can 
hear you. ... (Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You tell me under which rule you wish 
to raise the point of order. 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: Sir, the rule under which I 
am raising my point of order is, I69(ii), (viii), (ix) and (xii). 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Rule 169 ! 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: Yes, Sir. Rule 169 (ii). (viii), 
(ix) and (xii). May I elaborate my point, Sir? ...(Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You are saying rule 169. 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: Rule 169 (ii), (viii), (ix) and 
(xii). These are the sub-rules. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, what is his point? 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: Sir, I will elaborate it. The 
Motion says, "he reported statement". Now, it is an accepted 
fact that the so-called .eported statement was not made on the 
floor... 
246 

[18 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, it is about the 
admissibility of the motion. What the hon. Member is referring to 
is about the admissibility of the motion. Rule 169 deals with the 
conditions of admissibility. Once this Motion is admitted by the 
Chairman of the House, I think there is no scope for raising a 
question on the ground of admissibility. Therefore, my most 
respectful submission is, let us have the debate; the background 
is known to the whole House and let us not rake up this issue. If 
he has any other substantial points, he can raise it. How can the 
question of admissibility be raised now when the motion has 
already been admitted, bulletined and slated for discussion? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That is right. You cannot raise it. The 
Chairman has admitted it. So, ther e is no question of raising it. 
...(Interruptions)... Let me tell you that in order that the debate 
may continue in a peaceful manner, it is better you don't pursue 
it. and let the debate start. You can speak on it. 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: That rule is admitted; 
however, I have a point of order. ...(Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: l\lo, no. It cannot be raised. No point of 
order can be raised on the Chairman's ruling. ...(Interruptions)... 
No point of order can be raised on the Chairman's ruling. 
SHRI ADHIK SHIRODKAR: Sir, I am not disputing the 
ruling of the Chairman. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: No, no. No point of order can be raised 
on the Chairman's decisions or rulings. ...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the 
motion is admitted and it is set for discussion, with the consent of 
the Leader of the House. It can be admitted by the Chair, 
scrutinising the admissibility process. So far as the discussion is 
concerned, \t requires the agreement of the Leader of the House 
in regard to allocating the time. Sir, I would like to explain the 
reasons why we wanted to have this discussion under a 
particular rule. 
At the very outset, I would like to assure the hon. 
Members of the House, and my distinguished colleagues, thatI 
have no intention of transgressing our jurisdiction and assume 
the powers which the Indian Constitution has not vested on this 
House. I am fully aware of it. T herefore, I would not assume that 
power which is not given to this House. In this 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2000] 
connection, Sir, may I draw your attention to an observation 
made by no less a person than SarvapaNi Radhakrishnan, who 
happened to be the first Chairman of this House and the first 
Vice-President of this republic? When he assumed office, he 
was felicitated by the Members of this House on 13th May, 
1952. Then, he had observed, " There is a general impression 
that this House can't make or unmake Government and, 
therefore, it is a superfluous body. But there are functions, which 
a revising chamber can fulfil fruitfully. Parliament is not only a 
legislative but also a deliberative body. So far as deliberative 
functions are concerned, it will be open to us to make very 
valuable contributions." 
Sir, what was said forty eight years ago by an illustrious 
son of this country is equally relevant now. I must express my 
satisfaction, being one of the oldest Members of this House, that 
in its own humble way, this House has collectively contributed, 
through its deliberations, on many issues which have 
strengthened the democratic process; it has not weakened the 
democratic process and it has clearly established the fact that 
the Second Chamber has its role to play. 
On what do we want to have a discussion? A discussion 
about the propriety of the statement of the Prime Minister. I 
would come to the substance a little later. But, in the evolution of 
!he functioning of this House, we have created some very 
healthy precedents. One precedent, at least, comes to my mind, 
which was debated on these things itself. On 10th August, 1973. 
this House debated a motion under rule 170. The mover was Mr. 
N.K.P. Salve, who is sitting next to me. The motion was in his 
name. The complexion of the House was almost the same. The 
only difference was, the seat occupied by my good friend, Shri 
Jaswant Singh, was occupied by Shri L.K. Advani at that point of 
time. I am occupying almost the same seat, with a little 
difference. The seat next to me, on my rightside, was occupied 
by Shri Kamalapati Tripathi, instead of Dr. Manmohan Singh. 
The House discussed and recommended to the Government the 
setting up of a Commission of Inquiry to look into the allegations 
and counter-allegations against the then Prime Minister and the 
then Deputy Prime Minister. As  the Leader of the House and 
representative of the Government. Shri L.K. Advani said, "Sorry, 
gentleman, I can't accept these recommendations, because the 
law of the land, the Commission of Inquiries Act, provides that 
only the Lok Sabha, in respect of the Union Government, and 
the Vidhan Sabha, in respect of the State Governments, is 
competent to make a recommendation to this effect." We were 
unhappy. We felt sorry. 
248 

[18 December, 2000] RAJYA  SABHA 
We thought that we didn't have that power. What could we do? 
But, perhaps, history took a full circle. After twenty one years, the 
same Shri L.K. Advani--I don't know whether wittingly or 
unwittingly-vested that power in this very House itself, when he 
decided to set up a-second Commission of inquiry to look into 
the Delhi riots of 1984. Just one year ago, Sir, you will recolect 
that on the floor of this very House, while replying to a Starred 
Question, Mr. L.K. Advani, the current Home Minister, expanded 
the scope of the debate and sought the opinion of the Leader of 
the Opposition whether a second Commission of Inquiry could 
be set up to look into the causes of the Delhi riots. The right 
which he denied to this House in 1978, gave that right in 1999. 
The point that I am trying to drive at is that this way the House 
functioned. Therefore, we wanted to have a discussion where 
not only the Members of the House would express their views 
but their views should also get reflected in the form of voting. 
And that Rule 170 is the only provision which permits this House 
to express its opinion, to materialise that opinion in terms of 
voting, whether it will be mandatory to the Government or not is 
a totally different issue. After all, dissension is a part of 
democracy. Disagreement does not mean disrespect. tf this 
House disagrees with certain statements, certain observations of 
the Prime Minister, one need not necessarily conclude that this 
House is expressing its disrespect to the Prime Minister. That is 
not the intention. When both Houses were created, when

romanticisation of the 19th century universalist ideas, integrated

pages of history of the 19th century is enough proof that neither 
respect for all religions, nor the idea of unity of God-head in 
themselves could create seculari sm. Instead, they circumscribe 
the social consciousness within religious parameters and thus 
keep the possibility open for particularistic and antagonistic 
tendencies to re-emerge at opportune moments. This is 
precisely the weakness of the Indian notion of secularism. This 
is what I believe, because it keeps religions in play and
